course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the North and South in 1860 is a comparison?
choices: The North built canals and railroads because its cities needed to move goods
The South produced more cotton in 1860 than it had produced in 1800
The North relied on free labor, while the South relied on enslaved labor
The South seceded in 1861 after Lincoln won the election of 1860
questions.explanation: A comparison places two things side by side in the same category, here the labor system and economy of each section.
choiceExplanations: This explains a cause and does not compare the two sections.
This describes a change over time in one section.
A comparison places two things side by side in the same category, here the labor system and economy of each section.
This describes a single event in one section.
questions.distinguisher: The canals choice is close because it concerns the North's economy, but it explains why the North built transportation and says nothing about the South.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between abolitionists and many free-soilers?
choices: Abolitionists condemned slavery as immoral, and many free-soilers wished to stop its spread
Abolitionists wished to stop the spread of slavery, and free-soilers wanted it ended everywhere
Abolitionists defended slavery as a social good, and free-soilers opposed it
Abolitionists made up most of the North, and free-soilers were a small minority
questions.explanation: Abolitionists made moral arguments against slavery itself, while free-soilers stressed that its spread threatened free labor.
choiceExplanations: Abolitionists made moral arguments against slavery itself, while free-soilers stressed that its spread threatened free labor.
The goals are assigned to the wrong groups.
Abolitionists opposed slavery.
Abolitionists were a minority in the North.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed choice is close because it names the same two groups and the same two goals, but it assigns each goal to the wrong group.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between Stephen Douglas and Abraham Lincoln in their debates of 1858?
choices: Douglas opposed the Union, and Lincoln defended it in the debates
Douglas called for the end of slavery in the South, and Lincoln defended it there
Douglas sought the repeal of the Fugitive Slave Act, and Lincoln sought to strengthen it
Douglas favored popular sovereignty, and Lincoln opposed slavery's spread
questions.explanation: Douglas would let settlers decide, while Lincoln and the Republicans held that slavery should not expand.
choiceExplanations: Both men supported the Union.
Neither man took those positions.
The debates centered on the territories.
Douglas would let settlers decide, while Lincoln and the Republicans held that slavery should not expand.
questions.distinguisher: The Union choice is close because the debates took place on the eve of secession, but both men wished to preserve the Union.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity between the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854?
choices: Both repealed the ban on slavery north of the 36°30′ line
Both used popular sovereignty to decide slavery's status in territories
Both admitted a new state to the Union as a free state
Both created a stronger law for the return of those who had escaped slavery
questions.explanation: Both laws let the settlers of the territories decide, which was the idea of popular sovereignty.
choiceExplanations: Only the Kansas–Nebraska Act did so.
Both laws let the settlers of the territories decide, which was the idea of popular sovereignty.
Only the Compromise of 1850 admitted California.
Only the Compromise of 1850 did so.
questions.distinguisher: The repeal choice is close because it also concerns the territories, but only the Kansas–Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri Compromise line.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an advantage of the Union over the Confederacy in the Civil War?
choices: A larger population, more factories, and a greater length of railroads
A stronger claim to the military loyalty of Southern officers
Control of the cotton crop that British mills wanted to buy
The support of Britain and France, which sent aid to the Union
questions.explanation: The Union's greater manpower and industrial resources helped it to win a long war of attrition.
choiceExplanations: The Union's greater manpower and industrial resources helped it to win a long war of attrition.
Many Southern officers joined the Confederacy.
The Confederacy held the cotton-growing region.
Neither power gave the Union aid in the war.
questions.distinguisher: The Southern officers choice is close because the Union did keep the army and navy, but a large number of officers resigned to serve the Confederacy.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was true of both the Union and the Confederacy during the Civil War?
choices: Both relied on volunteers only until the war ended
Both paid for the war with gold and silver coins alone
Both drafted soldiers and faced protest against the draft
Both won diplomatic recognition from Britain and France
questions.explanation: The Confederacy passed a draft in 1862, the Union passed one in 1863, and both met resistance at home.
choiceExplanations: Both passed laws for a draft.
Both issued paper money.
The Confederacy passed a draft in 1862, the Union passed one in 1863, and both met resistance at home.
Britain and France never recognized the Confederacy.
questions.distinguisher: The volunteers choice is close because both sides began with volunteers, but they turned to a draft when the volunteers ran short.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the Emancipation Proclamation and the Thirteenth Amendment?
choices: The Proclamation was ratified by the states, and the Amendment was a war order
The Proclamation covered areas in rebellion, and the Amendment ended slavery
The Proclamation ended slavery in the border states, and the Amendment did not
The Proclamation followed the end of the war, and the Amendment came before it
questions.explanation: Lincoln issued the Proclamation as a war measure, and the Amendment, ratified in 1865, made abolition part of the Constitution.
choiceExplanations: The descriptions are reversed.
Lincoln issued the Proclamation as a war measure, and the Amendment, ratified in 1865, made abolition part of the Constitution.
The Proclamation did not apply to them.
The Proclamation came in 1863, and the Amendment in 1865.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed choice is close because both documents concern emancipation, but it assigns the ratification to the war order.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity between the Civil War and Reconstruction?
choices: Both left the Southern states in control of their own affairs
Both gave the Supreme Court the leading role in making national policy
Both ended with a lasting guarantee of equal rights in the South
Both increased the power of the federal government over the states
questions.explanation: The war brought a draft, taxes, and a national bank, and Reconstruction brought the Freedmen's Bureau, army rule, and new amendments.
choiceExplanations: Both brought new federal controls to the South.
Congress and the president led.
Reconstruction ended with rights taken away.
The war brought a draft, taxes, and a national bank, and Reconstruction brought the Freedmen's Bureau, army rule, and new amendments.
questions.distinguisher: The Southern control choice is close because Reconstruction ended with that result, but both periods began with federal action that limited the states.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following compares the promise of the Reconstruction amendments with the results by 1900?
choices: They promised land to freed people, and sharecropping gave them farms
They promised segregation, and Southern states soon ended the practice
They promised equal rights, but Black Southerners lost the vote
They promised the vote to women, and Southern states granted it
questions.explanation: Poll taxes, literacy tests, violence, and Jim Crow laws took away rights that the amendments had promised.
choiceExplanations: The amendments did not promise land.
Segregation spread in the South.
Poll taxes, literacy tests, violence, and Jim Crow laws took away rights that the amendments had promised.
Women gained the national vote in 1920.
questions.distinguisher: The land choice is close because freed people wanted land, but the amendments did not promise it, and most freed people did not become owners.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.
